name: ConsentX – Cookie Consent Banner for GDPR, DPDPA & Google Consent Mode v2
author: ConsentX

sections.description:
A cookie banner that works the moment you activate it, and holds your trackers back until visitors agree.

ConsentX shows a consent banner on your site, blocks third-party scripts, pixels and iframes until the visitor chooses, sends the right signals to Google tags, and records every decision in your own WordPress database so you have something to show if you are ever asked.

No account needed to start, and nothing to configure first: activate it and a compliant default banner is live on every page, asking properly and holding trackers until the visitor answers.

Why ConsentX

  • It works on activation. A compliant opt-in banner appears straight away, with sensible defaults for every region. Nothing to connect first.
  • The blocking is real. Trackers are held before they run, not asked to behave afterwards — a client-side guard catches scripts, pixels and iframes as the page builds them, including ones added by other plugins.
  • Your records stay yours. Every decision is written to your WordPress database. A free ConsentX account adds a copy held off your server, which is what you want if the server is ever the thing that fails.
  • It serves from your own domain. The banner is not a third-party script. A blocked or slow CDN cannot take your cookie notice off your site, and an ad blocker cannot either. (There is an optional setting to let ConsentX serve it instead, for anyone who wants one widget across WordPress, Webflow and Shopify. It is off unless you turn it on.)
  • It is cache-safe. No consent or region state is baked into cached HTML, so it works with WP Rocket, LiteSpeed, W3 Total Cache, Cloudflare and the rest.
  • It looks like your site. Ten banner layouts and six colour schemes, chosen from live previews, with every colour and every word editable.

How it works

  1. Install and activate. Your banner is live. Opt-in for EU and UK visitors, opt-out for the US, strictest model when a location cannot be read — decided per visitor, automatically.
  2. Make it yours. ConsentX → Banner: pick a shape and a colour scheme, edit the wording, watch the preview change as you type.
  3. Say what you use. ConsentX → Compliance: tick analytics, advertising, functional or performance, and generate a Cookie Policy page with a live cookie table.
  4. Check it. ConsentX → Overview presses your own home page the way a visitor would and tells you whether the banner is really in it.
  5. Optional: connect a free account for cloud-held records, automatic cookie scanning, consent history, data requests and managing several sites from one dashboard.

What you get, free

  • Consent banner — ten layouts and six colour schemes, picked from live previews; a full preference centre with per-category toggles; and a floating “manage consent” button so visitors can change their mind.
  • Automatic script blocking — third-party scripts, pixels and iframes held before consent and released the moment the visitor accepts, plus optional blocking of your own enqueued handles.
  • Blocked-content placeholders — blocked YouTube, Maps and other embeds become tidy “click to accept” boxes with per-service consent.
  • Google Consent Mode v2 — denied-by-default signals set before any tag and updated on the visitor’s choice. Cache-safe.
  • Region-aware consent — opt-in (GDPR, UK, EU, LGPD, POPIA, DPDPA) and opt-out (CCPA, Canada, Australia) resolved per visitor.
  • WP Consent API support — other consent-aware plugins can read your visitors’ choices through WordPress’s own standard, so they hold back when ConsentX says to.
  • Proof of consent — timestamped snapshots of exactly what you asked visitors to agree to, for each version of your policy.
  • Cookie-policy generator — a Cookie Policy and Privacy Statement with a live cookie table, plus [consentx-cookies], [consentx-manage-consent] and [consentx-revoke-link] shortcodes.
  • Consent records in WordPress — what your visitors actually chose, listed in wp-admin, with no account and nothing leaving your server.
  • Accessibility — focus-trapped dialogs, ARIA roles, full keyboard support and reduced-motion respect.

For agencies, hosts and anyone running more than one site

  • One dashboard for every site. WordPress, Wix, Shopify, Webflow, Squarespace and Framer in one place, with consent records, cookie scans and policy versions per site.
  • One banner design, shared. Set it once and it applies across the sites on your account — edit it in WordPress or in the dashboard, both show the same thing.
  • Connecting a site is one click. Approve it in ConsentX and you are returned to WordPress with the key already stored; no copying keys between tabs, no per-site account setup.
  • Nothing to install per client. The banner works the moment the plugin is activated, so a site is covered before anyone gets round to connecting it.

With a free ConsentX account

  • A copy of every consent record held in your ConsentX dashboard, exportable for an audit.
  • Automatic cookie scanning, synced into your local cookie list.
  • Consent history, data-subject requests (DSAR) and compliance reports.
  • Every site you run — WordPress, Wix, Shopify, Webflow, Squarespace, Framer — managed from one place, with one banner design shared between them.

Connecting takes one email address, and nothing is sent to ConsentX until you press the button.

Works with

Built to stay out of the way of the plugins you already run.

  • Caching and optimisation — WP Rocket, LiteSpeed Cache, W3 Total Cache, WP Super Cache, Autoptimize, Perfmatters, NitroPack, Cloudflare. No consent state in cached HTML, and our tags carry skip attributes so minifiers leave them alone.
  • Page builders and themes — Elementor, Divi, Beaver Builder, WPBakery, Bricks, Oxygen, Gutenberg and block themes.
  • Analytics and tags — Google Tag Manager, Google Analytics 4, Site Kit, Meta Pixel, Microsoft Clarity, Hotjar, Matomo, LinkedIn and TikTok pixels.
  • WooCommerce — store tracking is held before consent, including the Meta and Google Ads pixels that fire on product, cart and checkout pages, so a refused banner means a refused pixel. Cart and checkout behaviour itself is untouched.
  • Forms — Contact Form 7, WPForms, Gravity Forms, Elementor Forms: consent at the point of submission.
  • WP Consent API — ConsentX registers as the site’s consent manager, so plugins built against the standard get a real answer.
  • Multilingual — every string is translatable and the banner text is editable per language.

External services

This plugin can connect to ConsentX (https://consentx.io), the service this plugin is the
WordPress client for. What is sent, and when:

Before you connect — the plugin is fully working and nothing leaves your site. The banner,
the script blocking, the preference centre, the Consent Mode signals and the cookie policy all
run inside WordPress, served from your own domain, and every consent decision is written to
this site’s own database. No request is made to ConsentX from the front end of your site, and
nothing is sent about your visitors.

There are no exceptions to this, in wp-admin or anywhere else. Until 2.9.20 there was one –
the Plans screen fetched the public price list – and it is gone: that screen now links to the
prices on ConsentX instead of reading them. An install that has never been connected makes no
request to ConsentX at all.

(Until version 2.9.15 this paragraph said the opposite — that nothing was added to your site
before you connected — and it was true of those versions: the banner did not appear until the
site was linked to an account. That changed in 2.9.15 and this section had not caught up.)

When you connect an account — by pressing Connect a free account on the Overview or
Settings screen, which opens ConsentX in a new tab, or by giving an email address on that form
— and only then — your server
posts that email, this site’s domain, its name, a one-time code, and this install’s banner
settings (its layout, colours, logo URL and the lines of copy) and the names of its consent
categories, to https://app.consentx.io/api/public/sites/claim. The banner and category
details are what let your ConsentX dashboard show your own banner rather than a stock one;
they describe your configuration, not your visitors. ConsentX then makes one request back to this
site, to /wp-json/consentx/v1/verify, to check the code is really being served here: that is
what stops anyone from registering a domain they do not run. If the email is new, a ConsentX
account is created for it and you are emailed a link to set a password; if it already exists,
this site is added to it and the account holder is emailed to say so. What comes back is a site
key and an API token, which are stored in your WordPress options table. Nothing here happens on
activation, on a page load, or on any schedule – only when an administrator fills in that form.

After your site is linked, by that form or by pasting a site key into ConsentX → Settings,
these requests begin:

  • Your server reads and writes the banner’s design at
    https://app.consentx.io/api/v1/sites//banner — its layout, colours, logo
    URL and wording — so the design is the same one wherever you edit it. It is read on the
    daily sync and when you open the Banner screen, and written when you save there. It
    describes your banner, not your visitors.
  • Your server asks https://app.consentx.io/api/v1/me, /api/v1/cookies and /api/v1/consents
    for your account, your scanned cookie list and your stored consent records. These carry a
    scoped API token as an Authorization: Bearer header – a separate secret from the site key,
    issued to your account and stored only in your WordPress options table. Without that token
    these requests are never made.
  • If “push consent receipts” is on, a visitor’s browser posts their consent choice to
    https://app.consentx.io/api/ when they accept or reject: the categories they
    chose, the time, the policy version, and the data your ConsentX dashboard shows as a consent
    receipt. This is the record that proves consent was given, which is the reason the service
    exists. Turn it off in ConsentX → Settings and consent is stored only in the visitor’s browser.

  • Pressing Scan my site now on ConsentX → Cookie scan, or Start an AI scan on
    ConsentX → xScan-AI, posts to https://app.consentx.io/api/v1/insights/scan or
    /api/v1/insights/xscan with the same scoped token. That asks ConsentX to load your site’s
    own home page in a browser and report what it found; the address scanned is one of the
    domains already on your account, and the request carries nothing else. Your wp-admin then
    polls the matching GET for the result. Both are available only on a paid plan, and neither
    happens unless an administrator presses the button.

  • Your visitors’ browsers load the banner from ConsentX. Every page of a linked site
    loads https://app.consentx.io/api/<your-site-key>/embed.js, and that script fetches its
    configuration from https://app.consentx.io/api/<your-site-key> — two requests per page
    view. It is the same widget a Webflow or Framer site loads, and it is why the design you
    edit in either place is the one your visitors get. This was a setting until 2.9.20, off by
    default; it is simply what a connected site does now. An unlinked site renders the banner
    locally instead and makes neither request     — which is also the fallback if you unlink,
    so your site is never left without a banner.

The banner self-check is not an external request: it asks YOUR site for YOUR home page
(https://your-site/?consentx-selfcheck=…) and reads the HTML locally. Nothing about the
check, and nothing from the page, is sent to ConsentX.

Region detection never leaves your site: it reads the geo headers your own CDN or host already
sets, through this plugin’s own REST route. No visitor IP address is sent to ConsentX by this
plugin.

Using ConsentX means accepting its terms, and what the service does with the data listed above
is described in its privacy policy. Both apply only once you connect an account:

  • Terms of Service: https://consentx.io/terms
  • Privacy Policy: https://consentx.io/privacy

Disclaimer

ConsentX is software, not legal advice. Installing a plugin — this one or any other — does not
by itself make a website compliant with the GDPR, the CCPA/CPRA, the DPDPA or any other privacy
law. What those laws require of you depends on what your site does, who your visitors are and
where you operate. ConsentX gives you a banner that asks properly, blocking that holds trackers
until it is answered, and a record of what was chosen; the responsibility for your site, your
policies and your processing remains yours. If you are unsure what applies to you, take advice
from someone qualified to give it.

ConsentX terms of service: https://consentx.io/terms
ConsentX privacy policy: https://consentx.io/privacy
sections.installation:
1. Install through Plugins → Add New → search for “ConsentX”, or upload the ZIP via Plugins → Add New → Upload.
  2. Activate it. Your banner is live from this moment — opt-in for visitors the law requires it for, opt-out for those it does not, and trackers held until they choose.
  3. Open your site in a private window to see it.
  4. ConsentX → Banner to change the shape, the colours and the wording, with a preview that updates as you type.
  5. ConsentX → Compliance to say what your site uses and generate a Cookie Policy page.
  6. Optional: ConsentX → Overview → Connect a free account for cloud-held records, cookie scanning, consent history and data requests. Nothing on your site changes when you do.
sections.faq:
Do I need an account?

No. The banner, the script blocking, the preference centre, Google Consent Mode and the policy generator all work on a plain install, and every consent decision is recorded in your own WordPress database.

A free ConsentX account adds what one site cannot do for itself: a copy of each record held off your server, automatic cookie scanning, consent history, data-subject requests, and several sites managed from one dashboard. It is an upgrade, not a requirement. (Versions 2.7.0 to 2.9.14 did require it before the banner would appear. That was the wrong call and it is fixed.)

Where are my consent records kept?

In your WordPress database, in a table of the plugin’s own, listed under ConsentX → Consent records. Nothing leaves your server unless you connect an account, and then it is a copy rather than a move — the local log keeps filling either way.

Is it really compliant without an account?

The banner itself is: it asks properly, blocks before consent, offers refusal as easily as acceptance, and keeps a timestamped record of what was asked and what was chosen. That is what the law asks of a consent notice, and you get all of it free.

Your site is a bigger question than your banner, and no plugin can answer it for you. Compliance also depends on what your site actually loads, what your policy pages say, and who you are. ConsentX gives you the controls and the evidence; the decisions stay yours.

What a single WordPress cannot do on its own is survive its own server: if the site is lost, the records go with it, which is the honest argument for keeping a copy elsewhere.

Is ConsentX a Google-certified CMP, and does it support IAB TCF?

Not today. If you show Google AdSense or Ad Manager ads to visitors in the EEA, the UK or Switzerland, Google requires a certified CMP that supports the IAB Transparency & Consent Framework, and ConsentX is not one of those yet — so for that one case you need a certified CMP alongside or instead of this plugin. Everything else here is unaffected: Google Consent Mode v2 signals are sent natively and are a separate mechanism from TCF.

My site is a publisher running AdSense in the EU. Can I use this?

See the answer above — for EEA, UK or Swiss ad traffic you need a certified CMP. For everything else, including Consent Mode v2 for Analytics and Ads tags, this works.

Does it support the WP Consent API?

Yes. ConsentX registers as the site’s consent manager, answers wp_get_consent_type with the model your site runs, and publishes every decision through wp_set_consent(). Plugins built against the standard get a real answer instead of the “no consent plugin here, carry on” default.

Will it slow my site down?

The front end is one small stylesheet and one script, served from your own domain, with no external requests and no render-blocking fonts. Nothing is written into cached HTML, so your page cache keeps working.

How do I know the banner is really live?

The plugin checks for you. After connecting – and whenever you press Check my banner on the Overview screen – it requests your own home page the way a visitor would, with no admin session, and looks for the banner in the HTML that comes back. If your home page loads but the banner is not in it, you are told that, with the usual cause (a page cache built before you connected). If your host blocks a server from fetching itself, you are told the check could not run – which is not the same as a broken banner, and is not reported as one.

Where is the banner’s code served from?

From your own domain. The plugin renders the banner, runs the blocker and drives Consent Mode inside WordPress; only consent records travel to ConsentX. So a slow or blocked CDN cannot take your consent notice off your site, and the design on the Banner screen is the design your visitors get – there is no second copy and no setting that decides between them.

Does it block scripts automatically?

Yes. Known third-party trackers, pixels and iframes are held before consent and released on acceptance. You can also list your own enqueued script handles to block.

Is it compatible with caching plugins?

Yes. No consent or region state is written into cached HTML — the banner reads consent client-side and resolves region via a lightweight request — and our tags carry optimizer-skip attributes so minify/defer plugins leave them alone.

Does it support Google Consent Mode v2?

Yes, natively and locally: denied-by-default signals are set before any tag and updated on the visitor’s choice.
sections.changelog:
2.9.21

  • Fixed: Reports, Data requests, Categories, xScan-AI and Plans & pricing said “Sorry, you are not allowed to access this page.” These screens moved from the left menu into tabs in 2.9.20, and the way they were taken out of the menu also stopped WordPress finding them when it checks access. They open again from every tab and every Overview link, and the menu item they belong to (Records, Cookies, Scans, Settings) stays highlighted while you are on one.
  • Fixed: “Full report on ConsentX” on the Cookie scan screen opened a page that does not exist. It now opens that scan’s own report on the dashboard, and the xScan-AI button opens that run’s report.
  • Fixed: the Cookie scan screen could sit on “This scan is queued” with 0/0/0 and “No banner found”. Those figures came from a scan that had not run – or had failed – shown as if it had looked at your site. An unfinished scan now shows its progress and updates by itself, a failed or stuck one says so with a Try again button, and your last completed result stays on screen meanwhile.
  • Fixed: Google Analytics cookies (ga, _ga*, _gid, _gat) could be listed as Necessary. Necessary cookies are never held back, so they loaded before consent. They are now always filed under Analytics, on sync, in the cookie editor, and – by this update – in your existing cookie list.

2.9.20

  • New: a setup wizard on first activation. Three screens — here is the banner you already have, make it look like your site, and (optionally) connect a free account — then you land on the dashboard. Activating used to drop you straight onto the Overview screen, which answers “is this working” to somebody who has not met the product yet.
  • It runs offline. The first two steps use only what is already on your install, so a host that blocks outbound connections still gets you to the end with a banner you chose.
  • It does not come back. Finishing it, skipping it, or connecting an account by any route closes it for good — including connecting from Settings or pasting a site key, which are not the only ways to arrive set up.
  • Fixed: the Banner screen’s live preview was at the bottom of the page. It is meant to sit beside the pickers and stay there while you scroll; on any install that showed the hosted-rendering note, that note took the right-hand column and pushed the preview down below every card. The note is gone and the preview is pinned top-right, visible while you work through Layout, Colours, Text, Logo and Behaviour. On a narrow screen it now sits above the form instead of below it.
  • New: “Choose from Media Library” beside the logo field. It used to carry a sentence telling you to open your Media Library in another tab, upload, copy the address and paste it back.
  • Removed: the Opt-in / Opt-out “Consent model” selector. The Compliance screen correctly says each visitor gets their own law automatically, and it is right — the front end decides per request, so the selector changed nothing a visitor would see while appearing to be the decision.
  • Changed: ConsentX now serves the banner on every connected site, and the setting that chose is gone. It existed because, before 2.9.17, connecting could silently move your design away from the Banner screen. There is one design document now and both places edit it, so there was nothing left for the switch to protect against. An unlinked site renders the banner locally and contacts nothing — which is also what happens if you unlink, so your site is never left without a banner. The two “Cloud sync” checkboxes have gone the same way: they were three ways to half-connect a site, each of which broke a different screen in silence.
  • Nothing at all leaves an install that has not been connected. The Plans screen used to fetch the public price list, which was the one documented exception; it links to the prices on ConsentX instead. The “External services” section of this readme now has no exceptions in it, and links the terms and the privacy policy.
  • Changed: twelve menu items are now seven. Categories folds into Cookies; Reports and Data requests into Records; xScan-AI into Scans; Plans into Settings — each as a tab at the top of the screen. No page was removed and no URL changed, so every bookmark and every link still works.
  • Changed: the explanatory paragraph under almost every heading is gone. A merchant who has clicked “Reports” does not need to be told they are looking at reports, and the sentence was sitting where the answer to their next question should be.
  • Fixed: the Pro plan card listed the cookie banner, preference centre, Consent Mode, cookie policy and script blocking among the things Pro adds. They are free on every install; they appeared there because the card that used to list them — Free — stopped being drawn, which made Pro the first card and so the one the code treated as the bottom rung. They are now one “Free forever” line above the cards.

2.9.19

  • Changed: a banner edited in the ConsentX dashboard now reaches your site in seconds. It used to arrive when an administrator next opened the Banner screen, pressed Sync, or the daily sync ran — so on a site nobody logs into, not until the next day. ConsentX now tells the site when the design changes, and the site fetches it for itself. The message carries no design and no credentials: it is a knock on the door, and your site answers it with the same authenticated request it would have made on its next sync.
  • Fixed: page caches were never purged when the banner changed. The plugin has always asked WP Rocket, LiteSpeed, W3 Total Cache and the rest to flush when its configuration changed, and the banner’s own design never triggered it — the design lives in a table rather than in an option, and nothing fired the signal the cache integration listens for. So a site with a page cache could keep serving the old banner indefinitely. Saving the banner, and receiving a new design from ConsentX, both purge now.

2.9.18

  • Fixed: a change made in the ConsentX dashboard still did not reach WordPress. 2.9.17 added a guard so a scheduled sync could not overwrite an edit of yours that had not uploaded yet — but it decided which side was newer from the design document’s timestamp, and ConsentX only moves that timestamp when a plugin writes the document, not when you edit in the dashboard. So a dashboard change never looked newer and was never taken, which is the exact fault 2.9.17 set out to fix. The plugin now asks something it can answer for itself: does this site hold an edit that never reached ConsentX? If it does, it retries sending it; if it does not, it takes the shared design.

2.9.17

  • Fixed: your colours never travelled between WordPress and ConsentX. The two stored them in different places — ConsentX paints a banner from the website’s theme, WordPress wrote its own colors — and neither read the other. Picking a colour scheme in WordPress changed nothing on your dashboard or on your other sites, and recolouring in the dashboard changed nothing in WordPress. They are one store now, so a change in either place is the change everywhere.
  • New: your logo. ConsentX has always been able to hold one and show it on the banner and the preference centre; it was not part of the design that travels, so the WordPress banner could not have one at all. It travels now, there is a field for it on the Banner screen, and it is drawn at the same size as on every other ConsentX platform.
  • Fixed: the design only came down when you opened the Banner screen. The live site renders from a local copy, and the only thing that ever refreshed that copy was an administrator visiting wp-admin — so a banner edited in the dashboard did not reach a client site nobody logs into. It now refreshes on the daily sync, when you press Sync, and when a site connects.
  • Fixed: whichever side was edited more recently now wins. Opening the Banner screen used to overwrite your local design with whatever ConsentX answered, however old — so a save whose upload had failed was quietly replaced by the older copy it never reached.
  • Fixed: the preference trigger was two separate switches. ConsentX stored it as pref_button and WordPress as revisit, and the two never met, so turning it off in one place left it on in the other. One switch now.
  • New: the preference centre’s own heading and lead line travel too, so the hosted preference centre and this one are no longer headed differently on the same site.
  • New: an option to let ConsentX serve the banner. ConsentX → Settings → “Let ConsentX serve the banner” loads the same widget a Webflow or Framer site loads, instead of this plugin drawing it. The design is the same document either way, so the Banner screen still edits what visitors see; the hosted widget renders it in an isolated shadow root, which no theme CSS can reach. It is off by default and connecting an account never turns it on: with it on, every page view makes two requests to app.consentx.io, and an ad blocker, a strict content-security policy or an outage leaves the site with no banner and no blocking until they succeed. An early tracker guard is inlined in that mode to hold the common analytics and advertising scripts during the window before the widget answers.
  • Changed: the logo is only ever shown from an https address you set. Unlike the hosted widget, the plugin does not fall back to fetching your favicon from a third party — the front end still makes no external requests of any kind.

2.9.16

  • Fixed: the floating “manage consent” button never appeared. It is drawn with the banner, and the banner was only drawn for visitors who had not chosen yet — so the one control that exists for people who have already decided could never reach them. Anyone who had accepted or rejected had no way back to their choices. The setting said Show the whole time.
  • Changed: that button is now the one ConsentX draws on every other platform — a circle in your banner’s accent colour carrying the ConsentX mark, instead of a white circle with a shield emoji that rendered differently on every operating system. It is shown at size on the Banner screen, beside the switch that turns it on.
  • Fixed: “Last scan grade” showed a padlock reading “On Pro and above” on accounts that had paid. A site entitled to scanning but with no scan yet looked identical to a site that was not entitled, and the Overview tile read both as locked. It now says “No scan yet” and links to the scan. The same was true of the Open data requests tile.
  • Fixed: your plan was not read until the next day. Connecting an account stored the credentials and left the plan to a daily cron, so every paid screen stayed locked for up to 24 hours after paying. Connecting now reads the account immediately, and Plans & pricing carries a Refresh link. Disconnecting clears the cached plan, which it should always have done.
  • New: scans run inside WordPress. “Start an AI scan” and “Run a scan” were links to the ConsentX dashboard — the screen that advertises the feature sent you elsewhere to use it. Both now start the scan from wp-admin, show progress, and load the result on the same screen, with a button to write the findings into your cookie list. Your API key stays on the server.
  • Fixed: Compliance arrived pre-filled with values nobody chose. The organisation name and privacy contact address were filled in from your site title and admin email address, and were being printed on generated policy pages as the organisation holding visitors’ data and the address to write to. Saving anything on that screen persisted them. They are cleared on upgrade if they still exactly match what was filled in, the fields now start empty with placeholders, and there is a button to put your site name and admin email back if that is genuinely what you want. A policy page will no longer print a paragraph it has no answer for.
  • Fixed: the “External services” section of this readme still described 2.9.14 — it said no banner, no blocking and no Consent Mode ran before you connected, which stopped being true in 2.9.15. It also described a hosted-rendering setting that was removed in 2.9.14. Both corrected, and the two scan requests above are documented.
  • Changed: “Activate it and your site is covered” overstated what a plugin can do. The listing now says what is actually true — a compliant default banner is live — and carries a plain disclaimer, as does the FAQ.
  • New: an FAQ answer about Google-certified CMPs and IAB TCF, which ConsentX does not support. Publishers serving AdSense to EEA, UK or Swiss visitors need one, and finding that out after installing is worse than reading it before.
  • New: the first screenshots on the listing.

2.9.15

  • The banner works on activation. No account, no connection, no setup: install the plugin and a compliant opt-in banner is live, holding trackers until visitors choose. Versions 2.7.0 to 2.9.14 showed nothing at all until the site was connected to a ConsentX account, which meant most people never saw the plugin do anything.
  • New: your consent records are listed in WordPress with no account. Every decision has always been written to this site’s own database; the screen that shows them used to say “not connected” while that table filled up. The local log is your proof of consent, and an account now adds a copy held off your server rather than permission to keep one.
  • New: WP Consent API support. Other consent-aware plugins can read your visitors’ choices through WordPress’s own standard, so they hold back when ConsentX says to instead of falling through to “no consent plugin here, carry on”.
  • New: a listing banner and icon, and screenshots, so the plugin can be seen before it is installed.
  • Changed: the left menu no longer hides itself. It used to prune to two screens until you connected, which hid a working banner editor from everyone who had not.
  • Removed: the “Your banner is not live yet” warning on every screen, which is no longer true.
  • Changed: the description, the title and the setup steps now lead with what the plugin does rather than with what it needs, and the listing says plainly what it offers an agency or a host running more than one site.

2.9.14

  • Changed: the Banner screen is now the only place your banner is designed, and what you save there is what your visitors see. The setting that could hand the design to your ConsentX dashboard instead is gone, along with the three notices that existed to tell you which of the two copies was live. Editing the banner in your dashboard still works and still reaches this site.
  • Fixed: “Saved. Visitors still see your ConsentX dashboard design” after saving the banner. Saving the banner now updates the banner.
  • New: Compliance has a screen of its own, between Categories and Consent records. It used to be a second form at the foot of Settings, where its Save button did something quite different from the one above it – it republishes your policy pages and starts a new consent policy version.
  • Fixed: the organisation name and privacy contact email arrived pre-filled with your site title and admin address, which look exactly like answers somebody gave. They start empty, and the policy-page generators now ask for them instead of publishing a document that names a guess as your data controller.
  • Changed: each banner shape now sits in one fixed place, and the “Corner” control is gone. It applied to three of the ten layouts, so most of its answers did nothing, and the preview beside it never moved – Corner Toast, for one, drew bottom-right in the preview and bottom-left on the site.
  • Fixed: the live preview scrolled out of sight while you edited the text and behaviour below it. It now stays beside the form on wide screens, and scrolls inside itself if it is taller than your window.
  • Fixed: the ConsentX icon in the WordPress menu was blank. The stylesheet that paints it had PHP inside a nowdoc string, so the mark’s address was published to the browser as PHP source.

2.9.13

  • New: one banner, two places to edit it. Your design now lives in your ConsentX account, and the Banner screen reads it when you open it and writes it when you save. Change the banner here and it appears in your dashboard; change it there and it appears here. No syncing to start and nothing to click.
  • Changed: the Banner screen says which copy you are looking at. If your account cannot be reached it shows the last design it saw and tells you so, rather than presenting an old one as current.

2.9.12

  • Fixed: you could not get your WordPress banner design back. Several screens told you to change “Rendering mode” on Settings, and the control was not there – it only appeared on older installs, as a one-way switch to the hosted widget. Settings now offers the choice in both directions, so the instructions are true and the design you pick here can be the one visitors see.
  • Fixed: paid features showed a padlock on accounts that had paid for them, and opened anyway when clicked. The padlock was drawn whenever your account could not be read, treating “we do not know” as “no”. An unknown answer no longer locks anything.
  • Fixed: the Save bar and the live preview could slide under the WordPress admin bar on a narrower window. Both now track its actual height, which is not the same on every screen size.

2.9.11

  • Fixed: the ConsentX icon in wp-admin was a generic shield, not the ConsentX logo. The browser-tab icon on ConsentX screens is now the real mark, and the left-menu icon is a simplified version of it, drawn to stay legible at 20 pixels.
  • Fixed: the Overview could report “your banner is on your home page” from a check made hours earlier, after the site key had stopped working. A stored success is now ignored once the key is known to be dead, so the screen tells you the truth on the first load rather than after you happen to visit another page.
  • Fixed: reconnecting left the old warning on screen. The stored check describes the key you just replaced, so it is now cleared whenever the key changes — no more success message sitting next to “your site key is no longer recognised”.
  • Fixed: Consent records, Reports and Cookie scan opened with “nothing is wrong with your banner” and a raw server error underneath, when the real problem was that the site was no longer connected. They now say so plainly and offer a Reconnect button instead of a Try again that could never work.
  • Fixed: the plan shown on Overview could disagree with the Plans screen. Both now read the same source.

2.9.10

  • Fixed: the Overview screen said “Website connected” with a green tick directly above a warning that visitors were getting nothing. Both could not be true. The heading now follows the worst thing the screen knows, so a broken connection looks broken before you read a word of it.
  • Fixed: a dead site key produced two separate warnings – “key not recognised” and “your account could not be reached” – which are one fault seen from two sides. Only the one that explains it is shown now.
  • Fixed: the warning told you to reconnect in Settings without giving you a way to get there. There is now a Reconnect this site button on the message itself.

2.9.9

A large release. Everything below is new since 1.0.2, the version most sites
are running; the 2.x work was developed and tested outside this listing, so it
is summarised here rather than listed release by release.

  • New: banner designer. Nine layouts, six colour schemes, your own wording, and a live preview — all inside WordPress.
  • New: cookie scanning. Finds the cookies your site actually sets and keeps your cookie table in step with them.
  • New: consent records. What each visitor chose, when, from which country, and the reference you would quote to a regulator.
  • New: data requests (DSAR), with the statutory deadline shown on each one.
  • New: cookie policy and privacy statement pages, generated and kept current with your cookie list.
  • New: categories and per-category script blocking, including your own enqueued handles.
  • Improved: Google Consent Mode v2 defaults are set before any tag fires, so a visitor’s choice is respected from the first page view.
  • Improved: the banner follows each visitor’s own law automatically — opt-in for the EU and UK, opt-out for the US, strictest model when a location cannot be read.
  • Improved: an installation check that fetches your home page AND the banner script, so “your banner is live” means it is actually serving.
  • Security: all admin actions carry capability and nonce checks; all inline output goes through core’s enqueue and inline-script APIs.

Upgrading from 1.0.2 keeps your connection. Your site key and settings are read
from the same place and nothing on your site changes without you.

1.0.2

  • Fix: the connect callback URL is now built with a raw nonce. wp_nonce_url() HTML-encoded the ampersand (&), which corrupted the _wpnonce parameter on the return trip and failed the security check.

1.0.1

  • Fix: the “Connect to ConsentX” button now reaches the authorize screen. The off-site redirect host is allowlisted (it was being dropped by wp_safe_redirect) and the callback URL is no longer double-encoded.

1.0.0

  • Initial release: 1-click connect, Google Consent Mode v2 defaults, optional pre-consent script blocking, and manual site-key fallback.

short_description: Cookie consent banner for GDPR, CCPA and DPDPA. Blocks trackers before consent, Google Consent Mode v2, multi-site. Works on activation.
description:
A cookie banner that works the moment you activate it, and holds your trackers back until visitors agree.

ConsentX shows a consent banner on your site, blocks third-party scripts, pixels and iframes until the visitor chooses, sends the right signals to Google tags, and records every decision in your own WordPress database so you have something to show if you are ever asked.

No account needed to start, and nothing to configure first: activate it and a compliant default banner is live on every page, asking properly and holding trackers until the visitor answers.

Why ConsentX

  • It works on activation. A compliant opt-in banner appears straight away, with sensible defaults for every region. Nothing to connect first.
  • The blocking is real. Trackers are held before they run, not asked to behave afterwards — a client-side guard catches scripts, pixels and iframes as the page builds them, including ones added by other plugins.
  • Your records stay yours. Every decision is written to your WordPress database. A free ConsentX account adds a copy held off your server, which is what you want if the server is ever the thing that fails.
  • It serves from your own domain. The banner is not a third-party script. A blocked or slow CDN cannot take your cookie notice off your site, and an ad blocker cannot either. (There is an optional setting to let ConsentX serve it instead, for anyone who wants one widget across WordPress, Webflow and Shopify. It is off unless you turn it on.)
  • It is cache-safe. No consent or region state is baked into cached HTML, so it works with WP Rocket, LiteSpeed, W3 Total Cache, Cloudflare and the rest.
  • It looks like your site. Ten banner layouts and six colour schemes, chosen from live previews, with every colour and every word editable.

How it works

  1. Install and activate. Your banner is live. Opt-in for EU and UK visitors, opt-out for the US, strictest model when a location cannot be read — decided per visitor, automatically.
  2. Make it yours. ConsentX → Banner: pick a shape and a colour scheme, edit the wording, watch the preview change as you type.
  3. Say what you use. ConsentX → Compliance: tick analytics, advertising, functional or performance, and generate a Cookie Policy page with a live cookie table.
  4. Check it. ConsentX → Overview presses your own home page the way a visitor would and tells you whether the banner is really in it.
  5. Optional: connect a free account for cloud-held records, automatic cookie scanning, consent history, data requests and managing several sites from one dashboard.

What you get, free

  • Consent banner — ten layouts and six colour schemes, picked from live previews; a full preference centre with per-category toggles; and a floating “manage consent” button so visitors can change their mind.
  • Automatic script blocking — third-party scripts, pixels and iframes held before consent and released the moment the visitor accepts, plus optional blocking of your own enqueued handles.
  • Blocked-content placeholders — blocked YouTube, Maps and other embeds become tidy “click to accept” boxes with per-service consent.
  • Google Consent Mode v2 — denied-by-default signals set before any tag and updated on the visitor’s choice. Cache-safe.
  • Region-aware consent — opt-in (GDPR, UK, EU, LGPD, POPIA, DPDPA) and opt-out (CCPA, Canada, Australia) resolved per visitor.
  • WP Consent API support — other consent-aware plugins can read your visitors’ choices through WordPress’s own standard, so they hold back when ConsentX says to.
  • Proof of consent — timestamped snapshots of exactly what you asked visitors to agree to, for each version of your policy.
  • Cookie-policy generator — a Cookie Policy and Privacy Statement with a live cookie table, plus [consentx-cookies], [consentx-manage-consent] and [consentx-revoke-link] shortcodes.
  • Consent records in WordPress — what your visitors actually chose, listed in wp-admin, with no account and nothing leaving your server.
  • Accessibility — focus-trapped dialogs, ARIA roles, full keyboard support and reduced-motion respect.

For agencies, hosts and anyone running more than one site

  • One dashboard for every site. WordPress, Wix, Shopify, Webflow, Squarespace and Framer in one place, with consent records, cookie scans and policy versions per site.
  • One banner design, shared. Set it once and it applies across the sites on your account — edit it in WordPress or in the dashboard, both show the same thing.
  • Connecting a site is one click. Approve it in ConsentX and you are returned to WordPress with the key already stored; no copying keys between tabs, no per-site account setup.
  • Nothing to install per client. The banner works the moment the plugin is activated, so a site is covered before anyone gets round to connecting it.

With a free ConsentX account

  • A copy of every consent record held in your ConsentX dashboard, exportable for an audit.
  • Automatic cookie scanning, synced into your local cookie list.
  • Consent history, data-subject requests (DSAR) and compliance reports.
  • Every site you run — WordPress, Wix, Shopify, Webflow, Squarespace, Framer — managed from one place, with one banner design shared between them.

Connecting takes one email address, and nothing is sent to ConsentX until you press the button.

Works with

Built to stay out of the way of the plugins you already run.

  • Caching and optimisation — WP Rocket, LiteSpeed Cache, W3 Total Cache, WP Super Cache, Autoptimize, Perfmatters, NitroPack, Cloudflare. No consent state in cached HTML, and our tags carry skip attributes so minifiers leave them alone.
  • Page builders and themes — Elementor, Divi, Beaver Builder, WPBakery, Bricks, Oxygen, Gutenberg and block themes.
  • Analytics and tags — Google Tag Manager, Google Analytics 4, Site Kit, Meta Pixel, Microsoft Clarity, Hotjar, Matomo, LinkedIn and TikTok pixels.
  • WooCommerce — store tracking is held before consent, including the Meta and Google Ads pixels that fire on product, cart and checkout pages, so a refused banner means a refused pixel. Cart and checkout behaviour itself is untouched.
  • Forms — Contact Form 7, WPForms, Gravity Forms, Elementor Forms: consent at the point of submission.
  • WP Consent API — ConsentX registers as the site’s consent manager, so plugins built against the standard get a real answer.
  • Multilingual — every string is translatable and the banner text is editable per language.

External services

This plugin can connect to ConsentX (https://consentx.io), the service this plugin is the
WordPress client for. What is sent, and when:

Before you connect — the plugin is fully working and nothing leaves your site. The banner,
the script blocking, the preference centre, the Consent Mode signals and the cookie policy all
run inside WordPress, served from your own domain, and every consent decision is written to
this site’s own database. No request is made to ConsentX from the front end of your site, and
nothing is sent about your visitors.

There are no exceptions to this, in wp-admin or anywhere else. Until 2.9.20 there was one –
the Plans screen fetched the public price list – and it is gone: that screen now links to the
prices on ConsentX instead of reading them. An install that has never been connected makes no
request to ConsentX at all.

(Until version 2.9.15 this paragraph said the opposite — that nothing was added to your site
before you connected — and it was true of those versions: the banner did not appear until the
site was linked to an account. That changed in 2.9.15 and this section had not caught up.)

When you connect an account — by pressing Connect a free account on the Overview or
Settings screen, which opens ConsentX in a new tab, or by giving an email address on that form
— and only then — your server
posts that email, this site’s domain, its name, a one-time code, and this install’s banner
settings (its layout, colours, logo URL and the lines of copy) and the names of its consent
categories, to https://app.consentx.io/api/public/sites/claim. The banner and category
details are what let your ConsentX dashboard show your own banner rather than a stock one;
they describe your configuration, not your visitors. ConsentX then makes one request back to this
site, to /wp-json/consentx/v1/verify, to check the code is really being served here: that is
what stops anyone from registering a domain they do not run. If the email is new, a ConsentX
account is created for it and you are emailed a link to set a password; if it already exists,
this site is added to it and the account holder is emailed to say so. What comes back is a site
key and an API token, which are stored in your WordPress options table. Nothing here happens on
activation, on a page load, or on any schedule – only when an administrator fills in that form.

After your site is linked, by that form or by pasting a site key into ConsentX → Settings,
these requests begin:

  • Your server reads and writes the banner’s design at
    https://app.consentx.io/api/v1/sites//banner — its layout, colours, logo
    URL and wording — so the design is the same one wherever you edit it. It is read on the
    daily sync and when you open the Banner screen, and written when you save there. It
    describes your banner, not your visitors.
  • Your server asks https://app.consentx.io/api/v1/me, /api/v1/cookies and /api/v1/consents
    for your account, your scanned cookie list and your stored consent records. These carry a
    scoped API token as an Authorization: Bearer header – a separate secret from the site key,
    issued to your account and stored only in your WordPress options table. Without that token
    these requests are never made.
  • If “push consent receipts” is on, a visitor’s browser posts their consent choice to
    https://app.consentx.io/api/ when they accept or reject: the categories they
    chose, the time, the policy version, and the data your ConsentX dashboard shows as a consent
    receipt. This is the record that proves consent was given, which is the reason the service
    exists. Turn it off in ConsentX → Settings and consent is stored only in the visitor’s browser.

  • Pressing Scan my site now on ConsentX → Cookie scan, or Start an AI scan on
    ConsentX → xScan-AI, posts to https://app.consentx.io/api/v1/insights/scan or
    /api/v1/insights/xscan with the same scoped token. That asks ConsentX to load your site’s
    own home page in a browser and report what it found; the address scanned is one of the
    domains already on your account, and the request carries nothing else. Your wp-admin then
    polls the matching GET for the result. Both are available only on a paid plan, and neither
    happens unless an administrator presses the button.

  • Your visitors’ browsers load the banner from ConsentX. Every page of a linked site
    loads https://app.consentx.io/api/<your-site-key>/embed.js, and that script fetches its
    configuration from https://app.consentx.io/api/<your-site-key> — two requests per page
    view. It is the same widget a Webflow or Framer site loads, and it is why the design you
    edit in either place is the one your visitors get. This was a setting until 2.9.20, off by
    default; it is simply what a connected site does now. An unlinked site renders the banner
    locally instead and makes neither request     — which is also the fallback if you unlink,
    so your site is never left without a banner.

The banner self-check is not an external request: it asks YOUR site for YOUR home page
(https://your-site/?consentx-selfcheck=…) and reads the HTML locally. Nothing about the
check, and nothing from the page, is sent to ConsentX.

Region detection never leaves your site: it reads the geo headers your own CDN or host already
sets, through this plugin’s own REST route. No visitor IP address is sent to ConsentX by this
plugin.

Using ConsentX means accepting its terms, and what the service does with the data listed above
is described in its privacy policy. Both apply only once you connect an account:

  • Terms of Service: https://consentx.io/terms
  • Privacy Policy: https://consentx.io/privacy

Disclaimer

ConsentX is software, not legal advice. Installing a plugin — this one or any other — does not
by itself make a website compliant with the GDPR, the CCPA/CPRA, the DPDPA or any other privacy
law. What those laws require of you depends on what your site does, who your visitors are and
where you operate. ConsentX gives you a banner that asks properly, blocking that holds trackers
until it is answered, and a record of what was chosen; the responsibility for your site, your
policies and your processing remains yours. If you are unsure what applies to you, take advice
from someone qualified to give it.

ConsentX terms of service: https://consentx.io/terms
ConsentX privacy policy: https://consentx.io/privacy

upgrade_notice.2.9.21: Fixes five screens that refused to open from their tabs, the Cookie scan report link, scans stuck on "queued", and Google Analytics cookies listed as Necessary. Existing analytics cookies are moved to Analytics on update.
upgrade_notice.2.9.20: New installs get a three-step setup wizard, the Banner screen's live preview sits beside the pickers where it belongs, and the left menu is seven items rather than twelve. ConsentX now serves the banner on every connected site and the setting that chose is gone — an unlinked site still renders locally and contacts nothing. Existing settings are preserved and no URL has changed.
upgrade_notice.2.9.19: A banner edited in the ConsentX dashboard now reaches your site in seconds instead of waiting for the daily sync, and a design change finally purges your page cache — which it never did before, so a cached site could serve the old banner indefinitely.
upgrade_notice.2.9.18: Fixes the half of 2.9.17 that did not work: a banner edited in the ConsentX dashboard now really does reach your WordPress site, on the daily sync and whenever you press Sync.
upgrade_notice.2.9.17: Your banner's design now really is one design. Colours and the preference trigger were stored separately in WordPress and in ConsentX and never reached each other; your logo was not shared at all. All of it travels now, in both directions, and the live site picks up a dashboard change without anyone opening wp-admin. If the two have drifted apart, the side you edited most recently is the one that wins.
upgrade_notice.2.9.16: The floating "manage consent" button never actually appeared for visitors who had already chosen — fixed, and redrawn to match ConsentX everywhere else. Paid accounts no longer see a padlock on scan results they are entitled to. Scans run inside wp-admin instead of sending you to the dashboard. Compliance no longer arrives pre-filled with your site title and admin email, and clears those if they were never yours to begin with.
upgrade_notice.2.9.15: Your banner now works the moment the plugin is activated, with no account needed, and your consent records are listed in WordPress. Connecting ConsentX becomes an upgrade rather than a requirement.
upgrade_notice.2.9.14: The Banner screen is now the only place your banner is designed, and what you save there is what visitors see. Compliance has moved to its own menu item, and your organisation name and contact email are no longer pre-filled with a guess.
upgrade_notice.2.9.13: Your banner design is now shared with your ConsentX dashboard: edit it in either place and both show the same thing.
upgrade_notice.2.9.12: You can choose again whether WordPress or ConsentX draws your banner, and paid features no longer show a padlock to accounts that have paid for them.
upgrade_notice.2.9.11: The plugin no longer reports a working banner from a stale check, and screens that fail because the site is disconnected now say so and offer the fix.
upgrade_notice.2.9.10: Clearer reporting when a site key stops working: the screen now says so plainly and offers the fix, instead of showing a green tick and a warning at the same time.
upgrade_notice.2.9.9: A large update from 1.0.2, adding the banner designer, cookie scanning, consent records and data requests. Your connection is preserved: the site key you already have keeps working and nothing on your site changes without you.
